newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. agency says parts of North Korea without food.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency says parts of North Korea without food.

text.p: Parts of North Korea have already run out of food and despite recent aid donations more relief is needed to stave off hunger in the hermit state, a U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) officer said on Tuesday.

Rolf Huss, who monitors North Korea for the Rome-based United Nations agency, told Reuters on his return from a visit to the famine-threatened communist country that some government warehouses in the south were now empty.

"At the end of May some parts had already run out of stocks, mainly in the southern provinces. In the North (they are expected to run out) mainly betwen June 10 and 20," Huss said in a telephone interview from Beijing.

He said the food situation had deteriorated sharply since his last trip to North Korea in March, adding some individual cases of malnutrition were comparable to those he had seen during the Ethiopian famines of the 1980s.
"Since mid-March the situation has gone from bad to worse. We saw cases of malnutrition both among children and adults. You definitely see wasted people; very, very thin people," Huss said.
"You see examples of people as badly affected (as in Ethiopia) but not as many," he added.
The WFP launched a $95.5 million appeal last month to purchase and deliver 203,000 tonnes of emergency food to North Korea, where unprecedented flooding in 1995/96 devastated entire cereal crops.

Huss said the WFP was on target to raise the emergency supplies after the European Union last week announced it would donate 155,000 tonnes of food aid but he stressed the outcome of ongoing four-nation peace talks would be crucial.
"We have had a decent response (to our appeal). If the (peace talk) discussions result in donations we will definitely reach our target and perhaps go beyond that," Huss said.

The United States and South Korea, which is still technically at war with the north since the 1950-3 Korean civil war ended in a truce, have refused large-scale aid until North Korea agrees to talks which would also include China.
Early appeals for help from the WFP drew only a lukewarm response from international donor countries which feared that the food aid would go to Pyongyang's government.

Despite the increased contributions, Huss cautioned that the U.N. agency alone would not be able to end the food crisis and called on the international donor community for increased large-scale direct aid to North Korea to stretch into next year.
"I am very worried over the situation. There is very definitely a need for (increased) food aid to avoid a problem. I hope donors will respond to that challenge," he said.
"It is very important to keep (aid) going not only for June but after these months."
Huss said the critical period for North Korea would be from when food stocks ran out completely until the next harvest in October and November.
Although early indications were for an improved crop this year, he said many irrigation systems were still damaged and the possibility of renewed flooding in August was a constant threat.
"New floods may come in August this year as there is no room for water," he said.
